sessionTitle: From the Field: Accelerate Your Development for Microsoft Marketplace

announcements.name: The Azure Marketplace is now the Microsoft Marketplace
announcements.shortDescription: the rebranded marketplace serves ISVs (visibility and go-to-market support), partners (private offer selling and reselling), and end customers (ease of deployment and Azure consumption commitment credit)
announcements.longDescription: The Azure Marketplace has been rebranded as the Microsoft Marketplace, positioned as the way to transform infrastructure-as-code templates into trusted, deployable products for customers. The speaker, a Microsoft MVP working for an ISV, frames the marketplace as beneficial to all parties: for ISVs it provides visibility and go-to-market support for their solutions. The session's goal is to walk through taking BICEP templates and turning them into deployable Marketplace products.

announcements.name: Bicep visual designer in the VS Code Bicep extension
announcements.shortDescription: an experimental feature accessed by right-clicking a Bicep file to get an interactive, exportable graphical overview of declared resources
announcements.longDescription: The VS Code Bicep extension (recommended for code completion and authoring benefits) includes a visualizer accessed by right-clicking any Bicep file and selecting 'Open Bicep Visual Designer', currently an experimental feature. It produces an interactive graphical overview of all the resources the template will create, which can be dragged around and rearranged. It also supports exporting the visualization, a newer capability useful for creating documentation.

announcements.name: ARM Test Toolkit (ARM TTK) runs 49 validation tests
announcements.shortDescription: the same tests Microsoft runs on upload, so running them locally first prevents failed upload cycles
announcements.longDescription: The ARM Test Toolkit (ARM TTK) lets you test-drive your ARM template and Create UI definition locally before uploading the ZIP file to the Azure Marketplace. Running its cmdlets executes a set of tests—49 in this version—covering rules such as variables all being referenced and URIs being constructed in a specific way, plus tests for the Create UI definition standards and security. Because Microsoft runs these exact same tests when the ZIP is uploaded, running them locally first saves time and prevents failed upload-and-retry cycles; all 49 results should be successful before uploading.
